title: A teenage runaway turned to a Mountie for sanctuary. He had other plans
summary: Kim Budd spent much of her childhood on the run. When she thought she'd finally found a safe place to stay it turned out to be anything but, and the adults and institutions that were supposed to…

blocks.text: On a bone-chilling night in January 1983, Kim Budd, just 15, sits in handcuffs at the Riverview RCMP detachment in a suburb of Moncton, N.B.
She's run away from home — again.
"I spent the whole night with them," recalled Budd, now 59 and living in western Quebec. "They locked me to a chair."

There's no mug shot and no charges because the teen has committed no crime. But the officer who picked her up off the frigid street isn't sure what to do with this runaway, and worries she'll bolt if she isn't restrained.
Tired and uncomfortable, the girl sits there until the morning shift arrives. One of the Mounties who has just come in pays her special attention.
"The first time I ever laid eyes on him I had a cold pit in the centre of my stomach," Budd recalled decades later. "He was sitting on the desk and he kept looking at me and watching me."
Budd, with her dark eyes and hair cut in an '80s shag, glares back with a scowl perfected by teenagers.
Then the Mountie approaches with an unexpected offer. He tells her he and his wife run an emergency foster home for kids like her. Would she like to stay with them?
The teen, who has already bounced from abusive home to group residence to reform school and then back to the same abusive home, agrees.
"He just wanted to help me. That's what I thought," she said.

In fact, the Mountie would demand much more from the troubled runaway, and the shelter and security he offered her would soon turn into a new form of confinement. She would learn that none of the adults who were supposed to protect her — not the police, not the doctors, not the child welfare officials — could be trusted when she needed them most, and the more she cried out for help, the less anyone would listen to the terrible truth she struggled to tell.
RCMP officer accused of abusing teen foster daughter
Kim Budd was a runner. She ran away from adults, and often into trouble.

Born in a small town along New Brunswick's Miramichi River, Budd was the youngest of six children and the only girl. Her father took off for good a few weeks later, leaving the family struggling financially.
Budd describes a difficult childhood, including being molested by a neighbour when she was four.
"I had some issues with that growing up," she said.
Her mother later remarried a man Budd remembers as volatile, strict and abusive.
"The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember," she said. "I was about nine or so, he would start putting his hands on my breasts or between my legs and he almost made it into a game."
Budd's step-father denies the abuse, and it's unclear what her mother, a woman Budd describes as passive and unaffectionate, actually knew over the years. She did not want to talk to CBC.
Budd first ran away from home at 13. 'The physical abuse was as long back as I can remember,' she told CBC. (Submitted)
By 13, Budd was starting to act out. She shoplifted, drank alcohol, experimented with drugs and hitchhiked, earning the label "juvenile delinquent."
Budd says in reality, she was shy, vulnerable and often frightened.
"I had some anger issues, but I wasn't tough," she said. "I didn't care whether I lived or died. I knew it was risky."
By the time she turned 14, her mother and step-father had had enough. They called New Brunswick's social services and the girl was placed in a group home, then reform school.
After 11 months at the Nova Scotia School for Girls in Truro, Budd was sent back to live with her mother and step-father. But that didn't last long.
"I needed to make some changes," Budd recalled. "My parents needed to make some changes…. They never recognized what they were doing that contributed to my running away."
So she ran again, and that's when the RCMP picked her up.

Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for about five years when he first encountered Kim Budd. Due to his standing in the community, he and his wife were quickly approved to be foster parents. (Submitted by Gilles Plouffe)
In 1983, Const. Gilles Plouffe had been with the RCMP for four years and was already on his third posting.
Plouffe was fluently bilingual and stood over six feet tall with broad shoulders and a wispy mustache. As a kid he'd been an altar boy, a boy scout, an air cadet and a school crossing guard.
He married his high school sweetheart when they were still in their teens, and by 25 they were helping raise other people's children in addition to two young kids of their own.
In a system desperate for foster parents, the young couple was welcomed with open arms. He was an officer of the law, after all.
"I think they saw us as a blessing," he recalled in a recent interview with CBC. "They cut corners like you wouldn't believe. We didn't have any formal background check."
Soon, the Plouffe foster home became a handy option whenever the RCMP picked up a young person like Budd. They'd simply notify social services, and that was that.

Michel Cormier, a retired social worker in Moncton, N.B., stands near the Petitcodiac River in the early fall of 2026. Despite dealing with hundreds of cases over his career, he says he still remembers Kim Budd from the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Michel Cormier, a New Brunswick social worker tasked with overseeing the care of teens in the early 1980s, got that call the day Budd arrived at the Plouffe foster home.
Budd had been under Cormier's supervision during her months in group homes and reform school, and he can still remember her all these years later.
"She was a nice kid," Cormier told CBC. "I tried to respect her, not treat her like a juvenile delinquent — basically as a child that was in a difficult situation."
Placing Budd with the Plouffes seemed like an ideal solution.
"These were the perfect foster parents," Cormier recalled everyone thinking at the time. "This Disney kind of family, that everything was beautiful."
A recent photo of the house in Riverview, N.B., where Gilles Plouffe and his wife fostered children in the 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
Budd, a kid who had long dreamed of belonging to a "normal" family, settled in with the Plouffes and started Grade 9 at Riverview Junior High.
While her basement bedroom was being prepared, the teen slept on a pull-out couch.
One night when her foster mother was away, Gilles Plouffe came in wearing only a bathrobe and slipped under the covers with her.
"I kept falling asleep off and on, and he kept getting closer. And he had intercourse with me that night," Budd recalled. She remembers being afraid.
Plouffe apologized to the teen shortly after, telling her what happened had been an "accident." But the abuse continued, becoming more frequent and opportunistic.
"There was never a choice for me," Budd said. "He was my foster father and what he did to me that night, and the many times afterwards, was illegal."
While Plouffe disputes certain details, he now acknowledges he had sex on multiple occasions with the teenager in his care.
"It wasn't set out to be a predator looking for a prey," he told CBC. "I didn't mean to do anything bad, I just wanted to have a girlfriend."
Gilles Plouffe talked openly with CBC's Julie Ireton about his history with Kim Budd. He wore his RCMP-issue leather boots to the interview. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Now 69, Plouffe needed no convincing to talk openly with CBC about his history with Kim Budd. Plouffe's then wife, Budd's former foster mother, died in 2007.
During a lengthy interview, Plouffe showed no anger, hostility or concern. Rather, he appeared to welcome the opportunity to provide his own version of what happened in the foster home.

"It was a love connection," he insists. "And it's hard to say, 'Hey, you're a Mountie and you're supposed to enforce law and you're supposed to know better,' and all this kind of stuff. I know all that."
Plouffe acknowledged he was aware of the sexual abuse Budd had endured as a child and as a runaway.

"It's not like she hadn't done it before. OK, I said it. It's not nice to say that, but she did do it before," said Plouffe. "I was showing her that people could be gentle, that it wasn't like the truckers she had met while running, that she could be passed on as a slave from one truck to the next."
The way he tells it, he provided the teen with food, shelter, clothing and "good values."
And yet he was keenly aware that what he was doing to his foster daughter was illegal.

Every male person who has illicit sexual intercourse with his step-daughter, foster daughter or female ward ... is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.Section 153, Criminal Code of Canada c. 1983

Back then, Section 153 of the Criminal Code clearly stated that a man who has "illicit sexual intercourse with his foster daughter … is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years." (Today the crime falls under sexual exploitation.)
"I had the Criminal Code in the house, and I showed her," said Plouffe. "I told her, as a Mountie, I had no intention of going into jail. That's the last place any police officer wants to end up."
"He showed me in the book that he could go to prison," Budd recalled. "He just thought he was above the law."
The abuse continued. But almost two years into her stay with the Plouffes, it's Budd who would find herself in handcuffs once again, being taken away in a police car.
Two days after Christmas 1984, Budd, by then 17, got into a heated argument with her foster mother.
"She started going on and on about responsibility," Budd recalled. "She had been irresponsible in my view. She wasn't being a responsible wife and I had to have sex with her husband."
The argument escalated and the woman threw a slice of pizza in Budd's face, then ran to her bedroom.
Budd followed. She had had enough of the lying and sneaking around, and of her foster father's late night visits. She was going to reveal the secret.
"I was running to tell her that Gilles had been sleeping with me," Budd said.
But Gilles Plouffe was right behind her.
"He grabbed me and put the chokehold on me and he made me unconscious," Budd said.
When she came to she was handcuffed, put in the back of Plouffe's RCMP cruiser and driven to the Moncton Hospital.
Moncton Hospital documents from December 1984 and early 1985 detailed Budd's admission, diagnosis and discharge. CBC has redacted some private information. (Submitted)
Hospital documents from December 1984 confirm that Budd arrived in restraints and that Plouffe told hospital staff the teen had "threatened to kill his family."
"Foster father is an RCMP officer. He used force to subdue her," the emergency admission form notes. "He feels the death threats are real."
Budd insists the only threat she'd made was to tell her foster mother that her husband had been having sex with her.

The 17-year-old was admitted to the adult psychiatric ward where she was medicated, underwent tests and attended group therapy. The hospital psychologist noted that Budd was insecure, impulsive, angry and suicidal, and that she felt "unloved" and had a "strong need for affection."

A couple weeks into her hospital stay, Budd disclosed to the staff psychologist what was really happening in the foster home. Documents from the time refer to Budd's "alleged accusations" but provide no details.
"I just needed to get it out. I needed the sex to stop," Budd recalled telling the psychologist.
Then she told Plouffe what she had done. That forced him to admit the truth to his wife.

Budd spent three weeks in the psychiatric ward of the Moncton Hospital when she was still 17. She told a hospital psychologist here that her foster father had been abusing her. (Marc Grandmaison/The Canadian Press)
The psychologist summoned the Plouffes to the hospital for a meeting. Eventually, Budd was brought into the room.
"They told me never to talk to anyone about the abuse that had happened in their home," she said. "They made me promise."
Looking back, Budd says staff at the hospital never regarded her as a child, but as a mistress.
"I had a nurse reprimand me: ‘How dare you sleep with a married man?' So she blamed me for the abuse, and that's pretty much how I got blamed for what happened, instead of Gilles."
The teenager had endured two years of abuse in her foster home. She'd finally worked up the courage to tell someone in a position of authority. And then the adults colluded against her.
Plouffe said he informed child welfare authorities that he and his wife would no longer be fostering children, but no one reported the abuse to the RCMP.
"I didn't ask anybody to cover anything," Plouffe insists. "I don't know. They see me as a Mountie. What are you going to do?"
Budd models a borrowed outfit for an upcoming job interview. (Submitted)

In fact, in yet another incredible twist, Budd — not Plouffe — would find herself in trouble with the law once again, this time as part of a spurious murder claim made by her abuser in January 1984, shortly after she was hospitalized.
"She had told [us] that she had killed somebody," Plouffe told CBC.

While the details remain vague, Plouffe said Budd had admitted to him that she'd killed a trucker in the U.S. after he had "taken advantage of her." He told his superiors at the RCMP and an investigator was assigned to the case.
Today, Budd calls it all a fiction concocted by Plouffe to distract his superiors from what was really happening to her in the foster home.
"I've never killed anybody — never," Budd said. "Gilles made me go through and told me to tell them."
But at the time, Budd, still just 17, went along with the ruse.
"I was just trying to protect Gilles," she said. "It's hard to explain it now, but I was a shell."
RCMP files confirm an investigation in 1984, but no charges were laid and the case was quickly closed when no evidence was found to corroborate Budd's confession.
Still, the teen was now firmly under Plouffe's control, as though handcuffed once again.
Budd and Plouffe married in 1988 and moved from New Brunswick back to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que. (Submitted)
Budd was released from hospital in the winter of 1984 and went back to live with her mother and step-father. She dropped out of school and worked nights cleaning offices.
Before long, Plouffe, now separated from his wife, reappeared. He would turn up suddenly in his police vehicle, letting Budd know he was never far away.
"He was supposed to stay away from me, but he never did," she said. "I couldn't go to the RCMP because he was the RCMP."
Budd knew she couldn't run again.
"I believed he could have found me anywhere," she recalled. "I was afraid he was going to make me disappear…. He had weapons at the house, in his police car."
Eventually, she relented to his frequent calls. The sex continued.
"I can't explain the hold Gilles had over me," Budd said. "He didn't court me. We didn't go to movies or restaurants, he didn't buy me gifts. I was his toy."
Shortly after turning 18, Budd moved in with Plouffe and his two young children. When her former foster mother found out she became furious, and this time went to the police.
Gilles Plouffe tells his side of the story

The RCMP began an investigation in 1986, according to documents obtained by CBC. Plouffe's police colleagues set out to determine if the sexual relationship had started while Budd was still in foster care.
They never talked to the alleged perpetrator, however.
"They did not interview me. They interviewed Kim," Plouffe confirmed. "But they never asked me if I did anything wrong."

It's unclear whether the RCMP questioned anyone at New Brunswick's child protection services, which oversees foster care in the province. And yet both Plouffe and former social worker Michel Cormier confirmed that employees within the department knew about what had gone on in the Plouffe home.

"The people that knew, I imagine probably had the idea that it was not any of their business. So they didn't go forward with a complaint to the police like it should have been done," Cormier said. (He left the agency shortly after Budd's placement with the Plouffes, but later returned to work there part-time.)

New Brunswick's Social Development office is responsible for child protective services including foster care. Budd was a ward of the province when she was in foster care in the early 1980s. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
According to Budd, Plouffe coached her to tell anyone who asked that the sex had started after she turned 18.
"He kept telling me that if I told his lie often enough, it would become my truth," she said.
Once again, the teen lied for Plouffe and the RCMP wrapped up the investigation.

"The allegation that Cst. Plouffe had sexual intercourse with Kimberly Ann Budd while she was a ward of Cst. Plouffe is unsubstantiated. There is no evidence to support this fact and no way we will ever be able to prove this fact," states an RCMP memo from August 1986.
But Plouffe's association with this teen runaway and one-time murder suspect created a new problem for him: He was deemed a security risk – not because of anything he'd done, but because of her.

"His security clearance has been downgraded," states the memo. "We do not feel there is any further action to be taken at this point with the exception of verifying periodically if Budd becomes involved in her former activities."
Budd became pregnant with her first child at 19. She and Plouffe would have three sons together. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Budd was 19 when she became pregnant with her first child, giving birth to a baby boy in May 1987. She would go on to have two more sons with her former foster father.
"I was very trapped," she said.
With no proposal or engagement ring, Budd and Plouffe married in a civil ceremony in January 1988 at the Moncton courthouse. No friends or family attended, and Plouffe did not wear his red serge.
"They harassed him about it until he quit the RCMP," Budd said, suggesting that despite dropping their investigation, Plouffe's superiors may have had their suspicions.
Later that same year the newlyweds left New Brunswick and moved to Plouffe's hometown of Gatineau, Que., initially moving in with his mother.
There, years later during a therapy session for one of their children, Budd told the therapist about the origins of her relationship with Plouffe.
"She kept giving me cards to go see a women's shelter," said Budd. "I started looking at my marriage … how dysfunctional it was."

At 27 — 12 years after first meeting him — Budd finally left Plouffe for good. She took computer courses and eventually secured a job with the federal government where she remained for more than 20 years.

RCMP officer Sandra Lavallee interviews Budd at the national police force's Ottawa office in 2017. During the interview, Budd reported the sexual abuse she suffered as a teen in the Plouffe foster home. CBC obtained a video of the interview through an access to information request. (RCMP)
In April 2017, Budd sat in an RCMP interview room in Ottawa to detail her complaint against Gilles Plouffe for historical sexual abuse.
In a video of that interview, Budd's pain is raw. Through tears, she recounts what she went through between the ages of 15 and 17 in the Plouffe foster home.
"He told me that I couldn't tell anyone. Nobody would understand ... it was our secret," Budd told the interviewer.
Shortly after, RCMP Const. Simon Boucher of New Brunswick's Codiac detachment launched an investigation.
Kim Budd speaks with reporter Julie Ireton outside the RCMP offices in Ottawa where in 2017 Budd reported the abuse she suffered in the 1980s. (Turgut Yeter/CBC)

CBC obtained through access to information the interview video and close to 400 pages of documents related to the 2017 investigation. While much has been redacted, the police files note that Boucher searched "different databases" for witnesses including Budd's former social worker, Michel "Mike" Cormier.

"The attempt to contact Mike Cormier … were negative," the records state. "Cst. Boucher followed up with social services in Moncton, no one from their office are aware of a Mike Cormier that worked there between 1980 and 1990."
Yet CBC easily found Cormier through social media. He still lives in the Moncton area, and during several conversations shared what he knows about Budd's childhood.
Cormier said he would have given the RCMP the same information — including the open secret about what went on at the Plouffe home — had an investigator ever called to ask.
Despite the RCMP's claim that it couldn't find him in 2017, Michel Cormier was still living in New Brunswick and employed as a social worker at a Moncton hospital. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
The RCMP closed the investigation into Budd's complaint in August 2018.
"There is not enough likelihood of conviction," Boucher concluded. "The main issue in the matter is the reliability and credibility of KB because there is no eye witness to the alleged sexual acts."
But there was another eye witness: Gilles Plouffe. Yet the RCMP never contacted him, reducing what Boucher called a case of "he said, she said" to a simple matter of "she said."

Plouffe spent hours talking openly with CBC about his past, demonstrating that he's not shy to discuss what happened in his foster home in the early 1980s. But he said he was never aware of the RCMP investigation until told about it by CBC.
Once again, Budd had tried to tell the truth, only to be dismissed.
"There was evidence there that he had abused me. They just ignored it," said Budd.

Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa, reviewed Kim Budd's legal files. 'We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying,' she told CBC. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

"There's no other victim where we assume that they are lying about what happened to them. That is unique to sexual assault, still today," said Daphne Gilbert, a law professor at the University of Ottawa who reviewed the legal documents in Budd's case.
"We don't believe women when they come forward and talk about sexual assault. We start from the position that they are lying."
Gilbert thinks Michel Cormier's evidence could have made a difference.

"I am embarrassed for the RCMP that they couldn't find him," she said. "Even without him testifying, the RCMP speaking to him and hearing that she had disclosed her sexual abuse, I would have thought would have been a persuasive reason to lay a charge."
RCMP Const. Simon Boucher was "not able to do an interview" with CBC, according to the force's media relations officer in New Brunswick.

According to Sunny Marriner, national lead for the Improving Institutional Accountability Project, investigators displayed "textbook behaviour" when they claimed Budd was an unreliable witness because as a teen she'd lied, done drugs and run away.

"Children who are experiencing sexual abuse may withdraw. They begin to have difficulty attending school or engaging in activities. They frequently run away," she said. "It doesn't undermine credibility, it supports that something was happening to the child at that time."
'It wasn't abuse, it was love,' Plouffe said of his relationship with Budd when she was still in her teens and he was her foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
Decades later, Gilles Plouffe still frames what happened in his foster home not as abuse, but as a love story.
"It's wrong, but that doesn't mean we have to go and and really shove it down my throat and say that was really wrong, beat me on the head," Plouffe said. "It wasn't abuse, it was love.”
That's a story Marriner says she's heard before in her work with survivors.

"It is not love, it is exploitation," she said. "Many people will be familiar with the term grooming.… It means very slowly creating a bond with the person that you intend to exploit that makes them believe that the two of you are on the same team together against the entire world."
Looking back, Budd realizes the odds were stacked against her.
"He got away with it because he was in the RCMP, so it got covered up for him and he got protected and he'll never be charged," she said.
Budd, right, shows Ireton the statement of claim in her case against her former foster father. (Francis Ferland/CBC)
In the spring of 2019, Budd filed a lawsuit against the province of New Brunswick, the Moncton Hospital, the regional health authority and Gilles Plouffe.
"Plouffe was given the power and duty to discipline and punish the plaintiff, which he used to perpetrate the physical, emotional and sexual abuse," noted the statement of claim.
The lawsuit alleged the institutions were negligent and the hospital psychologist breached his fiduciary duty by failing to report the sexual abuse to the RCMP.

Those institutions denied all allegations, and in formal statements of defence noted that any injury, loss or damages suffered by the plaintiff were no fault of theirs. They also declined to talk to CBC about the case.
In July 2026 a judge at the Moncton Court of King's Bench heard a trial for damages against Gilles Plouffe. A decision is pending. (Michael Heenan/CBC)
There was no trial, and in 2024 the suit was resolved out of court. Details are not public.

Plouffe didn't defend himself against the claim and in November 2019 was found in default — the civil court's way of saying he didn't bring forward any evidence to deny the allegation that he repeatedly sexually abused, assaulted and molested Budd for two years, starting when she was 15.
This July, the Court of King's Bench in Moncton heard a trial for damages in the case of Kimberly Anne Budd vs. Joseph Yves Gilles Plouffe.

"I want his acknowledgement. I want some accountability for it," said Budd, who has been diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder, anxiety disorder and a persistent depressive disorder — conditions that will require treatment for the rest of her life.
Budd and her lawyer are still waiting for the judge's decision in the case.
Kim Budd says she hopes her family will now understand her past
Plouffe has never acknowledged that what he did changed the course of a teen girl's life, and no one has ever asked him to. Marrying Budd and having children with her didn't change anything.
For two years, between the ages of 15 and 17, she was a child and her foster parents were in charge. Institutions failed her, and worse, sought to discredit her when she tried to tell them the truth.

Gilles Plouffe's position with the police gave him privilege and standing in the community. The reaction of the systems intended to protect children exemplifies the entitlement he enjoyed as an officer.
It's why Budd feels she has to keep telling her side of the story, over and over again.
"Some people might call it revenge, but it's not — it's justice," said Budd. "I want the record set straight."
Budd's story is tragic, and repeating it is embarrassing and painful, but she realized long ago that she needed to stop running from it.
"I want my kids to hear it. They're old enough now they can process it … and they can make their decisions."
Kim Budd was a troubled teenager, a vulnerable kid whose imperfections placed her in a perfect position to be victimized over and over again.
Today, she's a survivor.
If you need help: Sexual Assault Centres, Crisis Lines, and Support Service in Canada
